title: Trying to Hold Hevel
opening: How much of our lives do we spend trying to hold onto something that was never capable of staying?
body:
Today I read Ecclesiastes 1:2–11, and for the first time I read through the introduction to the book. I was almost stunned by it. “Vanity of vanities! All things are vanity!” Written more than two thousand years ago, and yet I could have been reading an observation of our world today.

The introduction explained that the questions Ecclesiastes raises are aimed at those of us who would claim some absolute value in this life. Even wisdom is challenged, although foolishness is certainly not praised. What profit do we really have from all the toil we do under the sun? Even when there is profit, eventually death comes—the great leveler—and whatever we thought we possessed is left behind.

It is remarkable to me that someone living sometime around the third century before Christ could have possessed such depth of understanding and then somehow captured it in words. Even words themselves are limiting. We take what we see, hear, experience and somehow try to manufacture it into language. Yet whoever wrote Ecclesiastes managed to capture something about the limits of our existence that remains true thousands of years later.

The Hebrew word translated as “vanity” is hevel. It is something like vapor, breath or mist. Something is there, but try to grasp it and hold it and you cannot. Ecclesiastes also speaks of chasing after the wind. What an image of so much of human life. The things we try to keep change like the wind, yet we continue trying to make them permanent.

We work. We build. We accumulate. We learn. We establish careers, homes, reputations and some sense of security. None of these things is necessarily bad. But how easily we begin treating them as though they can give us something permanent. Eventually someone else has the job. Someone else owns the house. Someone else spends the money. Even wisdom cannot prevent what eventually comes to all of us.

The world around us has changed tremendously since Ecclesiastes was written, but perhaps human beings really haven't changed that much. We still want, compare, accumulate and seek recognition. We still think the next accomplishment, possession, relationship or amount of money might finally provide enough security. Our vanities change, but perhaps vanity itself does not.

Then I came to Luke 9:7–9 and Herod.

Herod hears everything being said about Jesus and doesn't know what to make of it. Some say John has been raised from the dead. Others say Elijah has appeared. Others say one of the ancient prophets has arisen. Herod says, “John I beheaded. Who then is this about whom I hear such things?”

Then comes this small sentence: “And he kept trying to see him.”

That stayed with me.

Herod was a ruler. He had power, position, authority and wealth. In that moment of his life, he possessed many of the things people spend their lives trying to acquire. Yet something was happening outside of everything he understood and controlled, and suddenly Herod was the one searching.

“Who then is this?”

And John the Baptist was there in his thoughts. Herod had ordered John's death. Whatever his power, he could not undo what had been done. At the time, he knew there was something wrong in it, yet he allowed the wrong to be completed anyway. I cannot know what remained inside Herod afterward, but I do know that power could not change the past. Money could not bring John back. Position could not answer the question now troubling him.

The man with the kingdom was trying to see Jesus.

Maybe Herod is not so different from us. We construct our own little kingdoms. Careers, houses, money, plans, accomplishments, reputations. Again, these things are real and they are not necessarily wrong. The problem may be when we expect something temporary to provide what only something eternal can provide.

Eventually something happens that reminds us how little control we really have. A job disappears. A body becomes sick. A relationship changes. Money comes and goes. Someone dies. A plan we were certain about collapses. What seemed permanent suddenly isn't.

Hevel.

And then the Psalm almost answers Ecclesiastes for us: “In every age, O Lord, you have been our refuge.”

In every age.

Before everything I have built, wanted, achieved or lost, God was there. Before Herod. Before Ecclesiastes. Before any of us. And He remains.

Ecclesiastes could see the problem of death with extraordinary clarity. No matter what we accomplish under the sun, death eventually comes. But we are reading Ecclesiastes from the other side of something its writer had not yet witnessed. Christ came. Christ died. And Christ rose.

Jesus did not come to make our little earthly kingdoms permanent. He gave us a way beyond them.

And yet I still chase after the wind. I still want security. I want things to happen the way I planned. I want to be understood. I want to hold onto people, possessions and circumstances as though enough effort might make them stay.

Maybe this is some of the folly Ecclesiastes recognized so long ago. We mistake the temporary for the ultimate. The house is real. The career is real. Money is real. Happiness is real. Suffering is certainly real. But none of these things is God, and none of them can carry the weight of eternity.

Perhaps that is why Herod's question continues to bother me: “Who then is this?”

For everything Herod possessed, he knew there was something here that he did not. And he kept trying to see Jesus.

Perhaps somewhere beneath all of our striving is that same search. We just don't always recognize it.

Maybe we don't need to understand every part of this existence. Maybe we need to recognize what is hevel and what is not. What will pass and what remains. What can be enjoyed without being worshiped. What can be lost without losing everything.

“In every age, O Lord, you have been our refuge.”

Maybe faith is finally opening our hands and admitting that we cannot hold hevel.

And perhaps when our hands are no longer clenched around what was always going to pass away, they are finally open enough to reach for God.
prayer: Lord, I spend so much of my life trying to hold onto things that cannot remain. I seek security in what I possess, what I accomplish, what others think of me, and what I believe I can control. Help me recognize the difference between the gifts of this life and the One who gives them. When I begin chasing what cannot satisfy me, turn my eyes back toward You. When something slips from my hands, remind me that You have not. Teach me to live gratefully in this world without asking it to give me what only You can give. In every age, You have been our refuge. Be mine today, and teach me to open my hands to what is eternal. Amen.
theme: The temporary nature of earthly life, the illusion of permanence, human ambition and folly, Christ as our refuge, and learning to seek what is eternal
